description: Loop optimisations decomposed. LICM, unrolling, vectorisation, strength reduction, induction variable elimination, loop interchange, tiling, fusion, fission. Each transformation has preconditions; running them at the right time + right level is the optimiser's art.

sub_mechanisms.name: loop_invariant_detection
sub_mechanisms.definition: Identify expressions whose values don't change across iterations. Definition: only depends on loop-invariant values or constants.
sub_mechanisms.why: Required for LICM. Computation that doesn't change shouldn't repeat. Standard analysis: walk loop body, mark expressions where all operands are invariant.

sub_mechanisms.name: induction_variable
sub_mechanisms.definition: Variable whose value follows a recurrence: i = i + c. Basic induction variables (counter); derived (i*step + offset).
sub_mechanisms.why: Foundation for many loop optimisations. Strength reduction replaces derived IVs with cheaper increments. Loop unrolling needs to know the step.

sub_mechanisms.name: scalar_evolution_analysis
sub_mechanisms.definition: Determine how scalar values change across loop iterations. SCEV in LLVM. Computes closed-form expressions for IVs.
sub_mechanisms.why: Powers many loop optimisations: bounds checking elimination, strength reduction, vectorisation. SCEV's closed-form representations let the compiler reason about loop behaviour symbolically.

sub_mechanisms.name: loop_unrolling_factor
sub_mechanisms.definition: How many iterations to replicate. Full unrolling: known small trip count. Partial: K-fold replication + remainder.
sub_mechanisms.why: Trade-off: unrolling reduces overhead + enables SIMD but bloats code (icache pressure). Modern CPUs benefit less from unrolling (good branch prediction). Vector-aware unrolling (factor = SIMD width) still substantial.

sub_mechanisms.name: loop_vectoriser
sub_mechanisms.definition: Transform scalar loop into SIMD. Each iteration's work becomes one SIMD lane. Requires: no inter-iteration dependencies, contiguous memory access, sufficient trip count.
sub_mechanisms.why: Major performance win on data-parallel loops. LLVM's LoopVectorize. Auto-vectorisation succeeds when alias + dependence analysis can prove independence; failures are common in pointer-heavy code.

sub_mechanisms.name: SLP_vectoriser
sub_mechanisms.definition: Superword-Level Parallelism: not loop-based but adjacent scalar ops. Combine isomorphic scalar instructions into SIMD.
sub_mechanisms.why: Complements loop vectorisation. Code like 'a[0] += 1; a[1] += 1; a[2] += 1; a[3] += 1' becomes one SIMD add. LLVM SLP vectorizer handles this.

sub_mechanisms.name: induction_variable_elimination
sub_mechanisms.definition: Replace expensive derived IV computations with cheap increment. e.g., 'x = i * 4 + 8' computed each iteration becomes 'x += 4'.
sub_mechanisms.why: Classical optimisation. Especially valuable on architectures with cheap add but expensive multiply. Modern CPUs have cheap multiply but the transformation still reduces dependency chains.

sub_mechanisms.name: loop_interchange
sub_mechanisms.definition: Swap nested loop order. for(i) for(j) → for(j) for(i). Improves cache behaviour or enables vectorisation.
sub_mechanisms.why: Cache-friendly inner loops. Matrix traversal: row-major data + j-outer-i-inner is cache-friendly; i-outer-j-inner is not. Interchange when valid + beneficial.

sub_mechanisms.name: loop_tiling
sub_mechanisms.definition: Replace loop with nested loops over tiles of the iteration space. for(i=0;i<N;i++) → for(ii=0;ii<N;ii+=T) for(i=ii;i<min(ii+T,N);i++).
sub_mechanisms.why: Cache blocking: keep the working set in cache. Critical for matrix multiplication, stencil computations. T chosen to fit L1 or L2 cache.

sub_mechanisms.name: loop_fusion
sub_mechanisms.definition: Combine two adjacent loops over the same iteration space into one. for(i) A[i]=...; for(i) B[i]=...; → for(i) { A[i]=...; B[i]=...; }
sub_mechanisms.why: Reduces loop overhead + may enable cross-statement opts. Cache benefit: data loaded once for both stores. Must verify no inter-loop dependency violations.

sub_mechanisms.name: loop_fission
sub_mechanisms.definition: Inverse of fusion: split one loop into two. for(i) { A[i]=...; B[i]=...; } → for(i) A[i]=...; for(i) B[i]=...;
sub_mechanisms.why: Useful when the body's per-iteration register pressure is high. Splitting reduces pressure. Also enables vectorisation when only part of the body is vectorisable.

sub_mechanisms.name: polyhedral_compilation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Model affine loops as polyhedra; transformations are affine mappings on the iteration space. Provably optimal for the affine subset.
sub_mechanisms.why: GCC's Graphite, LLVM's Polly. Compose tiling + interchange + parallelisation in one framework. Powerful for HPC + ML; computationally expensive analysis.

derivation_rules.name: LICM_amortises_invariant_computation
then: hoisting it out makes total cost O(1) vs O(n) iterations
derivation_rules.why: Per-iteration cost × N iterations vs one-time cost. Standard speedup. Limitation: hoisting must respect dependencies + may not be legal if computation has side effects.

derivation_rules.name: vectorisation_requires_no_dependencies
then: SIMD execution gives Nx speedup proportional to vector width
derivation_rules.why: Lane-N's input must not depend on lane-1's output (etc.). Alias + dependence analysis must prove independence. When proof fails, no vectorisation. Major performance opportunity gated on analysis quality.

derivation_rules.name: tiling_keeps_working_set_in_cache
if: computation has temporal locality within a region of size T
then: tiling with size ≤ cache size keeps that region cached
derivation_rules.why: Matrix multiplication's working set scales with tile size. Choose tile = √(L1 size) for max reuse. Standard technique in BLAS implementations; auto-tiling in polyhedral compilers.

derivation_rules.name: interchange_for_cache_friendly_order
derivation_rules.definition: If the inner loop's memory access pattern matches the data layout (e.g., row-major data + column-inner loop), interchanging the loops improves cache behaviour.
if: inner loop's memory access pattern is cache-unfriendly
then: loop interchange (when legal) gives cache-friendly traversal
derivation_rules.why: Row-major arrays prefer i-outer-j-inner. Column-major (Fortran) prefers the opposite. Wrong order: cache miss per access. Right order: cache miss per cache line.

derivation_rules.name: unrolling_pays_off_only_when_overhead_dominates
if: loop body is tiny + branch prediction is poor
derivation_rules.why: Modern CPUs with good branch prediction handle small loops fine. Unrolling helps when overhead per iteration (branch + increment) is significant relative to body work. SIMD unrolling (factor matches vector width) almost always pays off.
